basic_info.name: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (DPDP Rules 2025), notified as G.S.R. 846(E)
basic_info.description: The DPDP Rules 2025 are the operational regulations under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023), notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) via Gazette notification G.S.R. 846(E) dated 13 November 2025 (Gazette ID CG-DL-E-14112025-267650), and announced by PIB on 14 November 2025. They contain 23 rules and 7 schedules and commence in three phases: Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 (definitions, Data Protection Board machinery) from 13 November 2025; Rule 4 (Consent Manager registration and obligations) from 13 November 2026; and Rules 3, 5-16, 22-23 (notice, consent, security safeguards, breach notification, retention/erasure, children's data, Significant Data Fiduciary duties, cross-border conditions, data-principal rights) from 13 May 2027. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk is that from 13 May 2027 every Data Fiduciary must give a standalone, plain-language, itemised consent notice describing the personal data processed and every specified purpose, obtain free/specific/informed/unconditional/unambiguous consent limited to data necessary for that purpose, notify affected Data Principals and the Board of breaches (detailed report within 72 hours), define purpose-based retention, and honour access/correction/erasure/nomination/grievance rights with grievance redressal within 90 days. A derived kiosk summary is itself personal data and separate processing, so it is lawful only if its creation, storage and disclosure were within a purpose and data description actually itemised in the notice the patient saw - otherwise fresh notice and consent (or a Section 7 legitimate-use ground) is required.
basic_info.organization: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India. The Act is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted 11 August 2023). Regulator: Data Protection Board of India (DPBI), established under Section 18 vide G.S.R. 844(E) with head office in the National Capital Region and a strength of a Chairperson plus four Members (G.S.R. 845(E)); appeals lie to TDSAT.
basic_info.status: in force and phased - machinery provisions operative since 13 November 2025; Consent Manager registration from 13 November 2026; core Data Fiduciary obligations, rights and penalties from 13 May 2027. The Data Protection Board is legally established but was still unstaffed as of September 2026.

technical_features.what_it_does: The DPDP Rules 2025 prescribe the operational mechanics of India's consent-first personal-data regime and therefore directly govern how a MediKiosk kiosk may collect, create, store, share and erase patient data. The load-bearing obligations for Module C are: (1) Rule 3 notice - each consent request must be presented standalone and independently of any other information, in clear and plain language, with an itemised description of the personal data being processed and the specific purpose(s), a specific description of the goods/services provided or uses enabled, and a communication link through which the Data Principal can withdraw consent with comparable ease, exercise rights, and complain to the Board; (2) Section 6 consent - free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, by clear affirmative action, limited to data necessary for the specified purpose, with the request accessible in English or any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages; (3) Rule 4 Consent Manager - an Indian-incorporated company with minimum net worth INR 2 crore may apply to the Board to run an accessible, transparent, interoperable, data-blind consent platform, retain consent records at least 7 years, act in a fiduciary capacity to the Data Principal, and avoid conflicts of interest; (4) Rule 7 breach - intimation to each affected Data Principal 'without delay', preliminary intimation to the Board without delay, and a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours (or a longer period the Board allows); (5) Rule 8 retention - erase once consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served unless another law requires retention, retain processing logs and traffic data at least one year, give at least 48 hours' pre-erasure notice, with the Third Schedule's 3-year inactivity erasure trigger applying only to large e-commerce/gaming/social-media classes and not to hospitals; and (6) rights - access, correction/erasure, grievance redressal published prominently with a response window not exceeding 90 days, and nomination. Also relevant: Rule 12 with the Fourth Schedule gives clinical establishments/healthcare professionals only a narrow, purpose-bound conditional exemption from verifiable parental consent and the child behavioural-monitoring bar, strictly for providing health services, while security safeguards and breach notification continue in full.
technical_features.architecture: A statutory instrument, not software: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (44 sections, 9 chapters) operationalised by the DPDP Rules 2025 (23 rules, 7 schedules). Commencement is staged by Rule 1(2)-(4). The First Schedule contains Part A (Consent Manager registration conditions) and Part B (Consent Manager obligations); the Third Schedule sets retention periods; the Fourth Schedule sets child-data exemptions including clinical/mental-health establishments; the Seventh Schedule sets purposes for the one-year minimum log-retention duty. Enforcement architecture: Data Protection Board of India (adjudicating, digital-by-design), appeals to TDSAT, and a penalty schedule inside the Act (up to INR 250 crore for security-safeguard failure, INR 200 crore for breach-notification failure, INR 200 crore for children's-data violations, INR 150 crore for SDF non-compliance, INR 50 crore residual). The DPDP framework is in addition to, and not in derogation of, other Indian laws (Section 38), and where the DPDP Act conflicts with another law the DPDP Act prevails to the extent of the conflict.
technical_features.inputs: Digital personal data (any data about an identifiable individual, collected digitally or in non-digital form subsequently digitised), consent artefacts, notices, consent/withdrawal logs, sublicensee/processor records, breach facts, and retention schedules. For a kiosk this includes patient identity, demographic, card/ABHA details, conversation transcripts, digitized documents and any derived summary.
technical_features.outputs: Legally required artefacts: a standalone itemised consent notice, a consent record with timestamp/notice version, a Consent Manager consent artefact (if routed through one), a breach intimation to Data Principals and the Board plus a 72-hour detailed breach report, a published grievance-redressal and rights-exercise process, and erasure/retention logs. No clinical or FHIR output is prescribed - the Rules only constrain the data lifecycle around any such output.
technical_features.standards_compliance: The DPDP regime is the overarching Indian statute; health-sector processing is additionally constrained by the ABDM Health Data Management Policy (India-only residency, ABDM consent artefact model) and the erstwhile SPDI Rules 2011 (which the DPDP Act supersedes in treatment by removing the separate 'sensitive personal data' category). It is not an interoperability standard and does not mandate FHIR/SNOMED/LOINC. Mapping note: the ABDM consent artefact (HIP/HIU/PHR) is a practical consent mechanism but is not automatically a DPDP-compliant Rule 3 notice - the two should be reconciled, not assumed identical.
technical_features.offline_capability: The Rules do not exempt offline or on-device processing; because the DPDP Act covers personal data collected in non-digital form and digitised subsequently, an offline-first kiosk that scans paper records and builds a local summary is squarely in scope, and its local encrypted store still needs purpose-limited retention, erasure on withdrawal, a minimum one-year log retention, breach procedures that work without connectivity, and a way to deliver the notice and capture consent before processing. Offline operation is therefore a data-lifecycle and evidence problem (consent capture, versioning, audit logs, deferred breach reporting) rather than a compliance exemption.
technical_features.languages_supported: The notice and consent request must be accessible at the Data Principal's option in English or any language specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution (22 languages, including Hindi and other Indian languages); Rule 3 requires clear and plain language. This aligns with and reinforces MediKiosk's bilingual (Hindi/English) requirement but the statutory floor is all 22 Eighth Schedule languages.
technical_features.deployment_model: Applies to any Data Fiduciary processing digital personal data within India, and also to processing outside India where it relates to offering goods or services to Data Principals in India. There is no kiosk-, cloud- or on-premises-specific carve-out. A technology vendor operating a kiosk is not itself the Data Fiduciary by virtue of running software; the hospital that determines purpose and means is the Data Fiduciary and the kiosk vendor is typically a Data Processor, with the Data Fiduciary remaining responsible for compliance in respect of processing done on its behalf under Section 8(1).

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Not applicable - the DPDP Rules are a legal instrument, not a system with measured accuracy. The only quantitative standards are compliance thresholds: 72-hour detailed breach report to the Board, at-least-48-hours pre-erasure notice, minimum one-year retention of processing logs/traffic data, at-least-seven-year Consent Manager consent-record retention, and a maximum 90-day grievance response window; penalties run up to INR 250 crore.
performance_metrics.latency: Not applicable. The nearest timing obligation is the 72-hour window for the detailed breach report and the 'without delay' standard for the first breach intimation.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Not applicable in a hardware sense. Operationally, compliance implies a consent/notice management system with versioning, purpose-level consent storage, consent audit trail, withdrawal plumbing that halts downstream processing, automated retention/erasure scheduling, encrypted storage with access logging retained at least one year, and an incident-response capability able to produce forensic detail within 72 hours. Offline kiosks must provision local storage for these records.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: No adoption figures apply to a regulation. The Third Schedule's 3-year erasure trigger is keyed to classes with at least 2 crore registered Indian users (e-commerce, social media) or 50 lakh (online gaming); a hospital OPD kiosk is not in that class. The DPDP Rules' own impact is measured by the phased rollout, the Board's constitution and (as of mid-2026) the registration of zero Consent Managers.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Not applicable. Compliance is assessed by the Data Protection Board of India through inquiry and penalty proceedings (sections 27/33), and can also engage constitutional-court scrutiny (the Section 44(3) RTI amendment and Board-composition rules are under challenge before a five-judge Constitution Bench, notice issued 16 February 2026, no stay). Practitioner guidance from EY, KPMG, DSCI and law firms provides non-binding compliance checklists.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: This regulation sets the legal spine of Module C's intake-consent and output-disclosure behaviour. It matters in four concrete ways. First, it supplies the exact notice standard the kiosk must meet before it processes anything: standalone, plain-language and itemised, naming the personal data and each purpose - which rules out a single blanket 'I agree' checkbox covering intake, summarisation, physician sharing and ABDM upload. Second, it resolves the derived-summary question in principle: under Section 2(t) 'personal data' is any data about an identifiable individual, and under Section 2(x) 'processing' expressly includes structuring, adaptation, combination and sharing, so the generated summary is itself personal data and its creation/transmission is separate processing. Because Rule 3 requires the notice to itemise the data and the specified purpose, the summary is covered by the intake consent only if the intake notice actually described (i) creating a structured summary from the conversation, (ii) storing it, (iii) showing it to the treating physician, and (iv) any ABDM/FHIR upload - otherwise that is a new purpose needing fresh notice and consent, or a Section 7 legitimate-use ground (e.g., 7(f) medical emergency or 7(g) epidemic/public-health measures). The safe design is to itemise summary generation and authorised sharing as an explicit purpose at intake. Third, it fixes the retention/erasure and breach posture: erase on withdrawal or when the purpose is served unless another law requires retention, keep processing logs at least one year, notify patients and the Board on breach with a 72-hour detailed report, and publish a rights/grievance process responding within 90 days. Fourth, it clarifies the role split: the hospital is the Data Fiduciary and the kiosk is a Data Processor, so Module C should surface consent evidence and purpose tags to the hospital rather than assert its own compliance.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) a standalone, itemised, bilingual consent notice generated at the kiosk, with each purpose separately selectable (intake capture, document digitisation, summary generation, physician handover, ABDM upload, any secondary use) - never a single bundled checkbox; (2) a per-purpose consent record carrying timestamp, notice version and notice language, plus an equally easy withdrawal path; (3) a purpose/provenance tag on every field in the summary so a field's retention and sharing basis can be proven; (4) local encrypted store with access logs retained at least one year and an offline-capable incident-response plan; (5) automated pre-erasure notice (at least 48 hours) and erasure on withdrawal where no law mandates retention, separating 'delete-on-request' data from data that must be retained under medical-records/ABDM rules; (6) a prominently published access/correction/erasure/nomination/grievance process with a sub-90-day response. Reject or redesign: (a) bundling all processing into one consent; (b) treating the ABDM consent artefact as automatically DPDP-compliant; (c) any use of the captured data for model training, analytics, product improvement, or insurer sharing without fresh specific consent or a compatible-purpose basis; (d) assuming the kiosk vendor owns the consent relationship - the hospital is the Data Fiduciary; (e) waiting until May 2027 to build notice/consent plumbing, given the November 2026 Consent Manager milestone and the interim reputational/regulatory risk.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Key unresolved risks for MediKiosk: (1) The derived-summary question has no explicit regulator ruling - the definitional answer (it is personal data and separate processing) is firm, but whether it needs a fresh notice turns on how the intake notice is worded and whether summary generation is 'compatible' with the original purpose; this should be resolved by drafting the notice to include it and by legal review, not assumed. (2) The DPDP framework has no separate 'sensitive personal data' category and no explicit health-data chapter, so health processing gets no special-purpose safe harbour beyond the narrow Section 7(f)/(g) medical emergency/public-health grounds - routine, non-emergency summarisation still needs consent. (3) Rule 12's Fourth Schedule exemption for clinical establishments is narrow and purpose-bound (health services only; not analytics/profiling) and does not remove security, breach and minimisation duties. (4) Enforcement is currently weak but the compliance runway is short: the Board was still unstaffed in September 2026, yet the Consent Manager tranche takes effect 13 November 2026 and the core obligations (and penalty schedule) on 13 May 2027, and there is no announced grace period. (5) The framework is still moving - a constitutional challenge (Section 44(3) RTI rewrite and Board composition) is before a five-judge bench with no stay, MeitY consulted in early 2026 on compressing the Significant Data Fiduciary window to November 2026, SDF designation criteria remain un-notified, and Consent Manager interoperability standards are unpublished - so any consent architecture should be versioned and adaptable. (6) The Consent Manager / RBI Account Aggregator overlap is unresolved and may complicate any health-data consent-routing design. (7) Consent withdrawal collides with clinical continuity of care and medico-legal retention, so retention/erasure must be segmented rather than flat.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: The DPDP Rules do not compete with MediKiosk; they constrain and certify it. MediKiosk's intended differentiators are largely aligned with the regulation and can be turned into compliance evidence: offline-first and India-resident processing satisfies the storage-limitation and any localisation posture; per-field provenance maps directly onto Rule 3's itemised-data and purpose requirements; physician attestation supports completeness/accuracy duties under Section 8(3) when data is used to make a decision or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary; and bilingual output can be extended to the statutory 22-language notice floor. The differentiation that DPDP actively rewards is evidence quality: a kiosk that can produce a versioned, purpose-tagged, bilingual consent record with withdrawal plumbing, a field-level provenance trail, and an offline breach/retention plan is meaningfully ahead of a cloud intake app that only shows a privacy policy. The main erosion risk is complacency - a bundled 'hospital consent' or relying on ABDM consent alone would fail the standalone/itemised standard and forfeit that advantage. Net: compliance is a tailwind for MediKiosk's 'trustworthy local capture' story provided summary generation and authorised sharing are itemised at intake.

business_info.license: Not applicable - the DPDP Rules 2025 are a statutory instrument under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, published in the Gazette of India (G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025; corrigenda G.S.R. 892(E), December 2025). There is no software licence; compliance is mandatory for in-scope Data Fiduciaries.
business_info.pricing: No licence fee. The economic cost is compliance and risk: penalties under the Act's Schedule run up to INR 250 crore for failure to take reasonable security safeguards, up to INR 200 crore for failure to notify a breach, up to INR 200 crore for children's-data violations, up to INR 150 crore for SDF non-compliance, and up to INR 50 crore for residual contraventions. A Consent Manager applicant must itself have minimum net worth INR 2 crore.
business_info.funding: Not applicable - a Government of India / MeitY instrument, funded through the Union Budget; the Data Protection Board of India is a statutory body funded by the State.
business_info.commercial_status: Mandatory government regulation. Phase 1 (Board machinery) is operative; Phase 2 (Consent Managers) takes effect 13 November 2026; Phase 3 (core Data Fiduciary obligations and penalties) takes effect 13 May 2027. As of September 2026 the Board had no appointed Chairperson or Members and no Consent Managers were registered, so no penalties are yet being levied.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: There is no competing Indian statute - the DPDP Act/Rules supersede the IT Act SPDI Rules 2011 as the general data-protection regime. For comparative design the relevant analogues are the EU GDPR (special-category health data, DPIA, legitimate interests) and the US HIPAA (health-specific privacy/security), plus India's sectoral layers that continue to operate alongside DPDP: the ABDM Health Data Management Policy, the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, the Drugs & Cosmetics Act / MDR-2017 (SaMD), and the Indian Medical Council professional-conduct retention norms. The RBI Account Aggregator framework is an adjacent, more mature consent-manager ecosystem whose overlap with DPDP Consent Managers is now the subject of active legal debate.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: The Rules interoperate, in practice, with: the ABDM consent framework (HIE-CM consent artefacts, HIP/HIU/PHR roles, Health Locker) which a kiosk will sit inside at a hospital; the Data Protection Board of India's digital complaint/appeals machinery; CERT-In incident-reporting obligations; and any registered Consent Manager chosen to route consent. For MediKiosk the practical integration is ABDM consent + a DPDP-compliant notice, not either alone.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Procurement and programme tailwinds favour DPDP-aligned products: government and large-hospital tenders increasingly expect ABDM conformance and privacy-by-design, and the Ministry's framing is deliberately innovation-friendly ('facilitative compliance regime for startups and smaller enterprises') with an 18-month runway. The main ecosystem risks are institutional and interpretive: the Data Protection Board is unstaffed (recruitment only opened May-June 2026); Consent Manager interoperability standards are unpublished; MeitY consulted in 2026 on accelerating SDF duties to November 2026 with SDF criteria still un-notified; and the Consent Manager vs Account Aggregator divide is unresolved. Health-tech guidance published through 2026 (Interlegal, eQomply, KSK) converges on data mapping, granular consent, data segmentation for retention, and treating clinical consent separately from data-processing consent - which is exactly the Module C consent design surface.

history.release_date: Draft DPDP Rules published 3 January 2025 as G.S.R. 02(E) for a 45-day consultation; final DPDP Rules 2025 notified 13 November 2025 as G.S.R. 846(E) and announced by PIB on 14 November 2025. The parent DPDP Act, 2023 received assent on 11 August 2023.
history.key_milestones: 11 Aug 2023 - DPDP Act, 2023 enacted (Act 22 of 2023). 3 Jan 2025 - draft Rules (G.S.R. 02(E)) published for public comment; consultations held in Delhi, Mumbai, Guwahati, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai. 13 Nov 2025 - final Rules notified (G.S.R. 846(E)); G.S.R. 844(E) establishes the Data Protection Board of India; G.S.R. 845(E) fixes it at a Chairperson plus four Members. 14 Nov 2025 - PIB announces full operationalisation and the 18-month phased timeline. Dec 2025 - corrigenda G.S.R. 892(E) correct eight points of the Rules text. Phase-2 date 13 Nov 2026 (Consent Manager registration); Phase-3 date 13 May 2027 (core obligations and penalties).
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Within roughly March-September 2026: (1) the Data Protection Board remained unstaffed - MeitY's circular of 6 May 2026 invited applications for the Chairperson and four Members, with the recruitment advertisement published in Employment News on 6 June 2026, and no appointments announced as of September 2026 (see Judicio's 21 July 2026 tracker and LiveLaw's 1 August 2026 analysis). (2) The constitutional challenge to Section 44(3)'s RTI amendment (and related Board-composition rules) was referred to a five-judge Constitution Bench on 16 February 2026; notice was issued and no interim stay granted, so all commencement dates continue to run. (3) MeitY consulted in early 2026 on compressing the Significant Data Fiduciary compliance window to 12 months (November 2026); no gazette amendment had issued and SDF designation criteria remained un-notified as of July 2026. (4) The Consent Manager framework came under active scrutiny ahead of its 14 November 2026 effect date, including a 16 September 2026 LiveLaw analysis of the unresolved Consent Manager vs RBI Account Aggregator overlap (both require INR 2 crore capital; RBI governance is stricter; the Board's interoperability standards remain unpublished) and a 3 July 2026 Candour Legal analysis warning that the registering authority was not yet functional. (5) A body of healthcare-specific DPDP compliance guidance appeared through 2026 (Interlegal, 10 Aug 2026; eQomply, 24 Jul 2026; KSK, 10 Aug 2026), emphasising that the DPDPA has no sensitive-data category, that clinical consent and data-processing consent are separate, that granular purpose-level consent is required, and that routine care (not just emergencies) needs consent.

market_positioning.target_users: All Data Fiduciaries processing digital personal data in India, including hospitals, clinics, diagnostic centres, telemedicine and health-tech platforms, pharmacies, insurers and their Data Processors; Data Principals are all individuals whose data is processed, with special provisions for children and persons with disabilities. Consent Managers are a distinct regulated applicant class (Indian company, net worth at least INR 2 crore).
market_positioning.market_segment: India data protection and privacy compliance, cutting across every sector; within MediKiosk's space it is the intake-consent, data-lifecycle and breach-notification layer that sits around ABDM/FHIR clinical interoperability.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: The Government frames the Rules as a citizen-focused, innovation-friendly framework built on the SARAL design (Simple, Accessible, Rational, Actionable) with seven principles - consent and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security safeguards and accountability - and a deliberately phased 18-month runway so that protection of citizens' privacy advances alongside a facilitative regime for startups and smaller enterprises.
